evals.prompt: We build Trellisway, a workflow automation API. Northbridge Freight - our biggest prospect, around $400k ARR if it closes - told us last week that their procurement team won't sign unless their integration engineers can get certified on our platform. Our CRO approved $80k for this fiscal year to make it happen, nothing committed beyond that. The team is me (DevRel lead, maybe 10 hours a week on this) and one solutions engineer who can give 5 hours. I was thinking we write about 60 multiple choice questions, set the pass mark at 70%, and launch in Q1. What's the best way to build this out?
evals.expected_output: A refusal to recommend proctored certification, a badge-rung recommendation instead, the three promotion conditions named with the failing ones identified, an observable certification trigger, and a rejection of the 70% pass mark as indefensible without a standard-setting study.
expectations: States a gate verdict in one sentence that names the evidence behind it and the cheaper alternative rejected
Recommends the completion or skill badge rung rather than proctored certification

Names all three conditions that would promote certification: a named buyer or partner contract counting certified heads, a funded second-year recertification cycle, and one person owning the item bank indefinitely
Identifies which of those three conditions Trellisway fails, covering the single-fiscal-year funding and the absence of permanent item-bank ownership
Writes the escalation trigger to certification as an observable condition rather than a date or a stated intention
Rejects the 70% pass mark as indefensible without a standard-setting study
Names at least one standard-setting method among modified Angoff, bookmark, or contrasting groups
States the standard-setting panel size as 5 to 15 subject-matter experts
Does not present a syllabus, course outline, module list or lesson content
Deletes the rungs the answers rule out rather than listing them as later options
Requires one named owner with weekly hours rather than a team label
Frames the badge rung as adding permanent issuance, verification and disputes obligations, not a one-time cost

evals.prompt: Hey - Quillstone here, we make an observability SDK, about 2,400 active orgs. Over three years we've published 41 tutorials and 12 videos and they sit as a flat list on our docs site. New users email us asking where do I start basically every week. I have a board review in 8 weeks where I need to show something concrete on developer enablement. Realistically I have one technical writer at about 8 hours a week and no budget for a new hire, now or later. What should we build?
evals.expected_output: A curated learning path recommendation, the efficiency ordering stated explicitly with ad-hoc content above badge, the rungs deleted by the capacity ceiling, and an observable escalation trigger to the curriculum rung.
expectations: Recommends the curated learning path rung
States the efficiency ordering explicitly, with the curated learning path first
Places ad-hoc content above the badge rung on the efficiency ordering
States that value and effort both put certification first, and that efficiency is the ordering that disagrees with both
Says the 8-week board review date promoted the curated path
Says the one-part-time-person capacity ceiling deletes every rung above the curated path
Deletes those higher rungs rather than parking them at the bottom of a list as later options
Gives the curated path's effort as an order of magnitude such as a day or two to curate plus a re-order per release, not a precise cost figure
Notes the curated path is reversible by deleting a page
Writes the escalation trigger to the curriculum rung as an observable condition, such as learners finishing the path and still being unable to do the job
Names the curated path's failure mode: a link list dressed as a curriculum with no evidence anyone finished it
Labels the five-rung ladder as this collection's own synthesis rather than a certified or published maturity model

evals.prompt: Vantahold here - we do a payments reconciliation API. Support volume is up 3x in six months and our VP wants us to build a developer academy. Looking at the ticket data: the biggest cluster is people asking which endpoint returns settlement batches, which is documented, page 4 of the API reference. Second biggest is people passing an expired token, getting a generic 400 back, and filing a ticket. Separately, 62% of new signups never complete a first successful API call. And one customer's platform team asked us for a training session last month. Can you put together the academy plan?
evals.expected_output: A gate verdict refusing the academy, with each evidence cluster routed to its cheaper fix: docs information architecture, quickstart and onboarding, product and error-message design, and a one-off workshop plus recording.
expectations: Returns a gate verdict that education is not the right fix for the evidence presented
States that verdict in one sentence with the evidence behind it
Names documentation information architecture as the fix for answers that exist but cannot be found
Names quickstart and onboarding as the fix for users failing at first success, rather than a course
Names product and error-message design as the fix for the expired-token case, on the grounds the API could refuse the misuse
Recommends a live workshop plus a recording, not a curriculum, for the single team that asked once
Distinguishes procedural support questions from conceptual misunderstandings, and notes only the conceptual cluster would justify a program
Does not produce a competency map or module list
Does not recommend a badge or a certification
Does not propose buying or evaluating an LMS
Routes the docs and quickstart fixes to the named sibling skills rather than performing them here
Names at least one observable condition that would re-open the education gate later

evals.prompt:
Working on the curriculum for Perigee Academy - Perigee is our data catalog product. Here's the draft module list I put together from our product nav:

Module 1: Dashboard overview
Module 2: Projects and workspaces
Module 3: Webhooks
Module 4: Billing and plans
Module 5: API keys
Module 6: Integrations directory
Module 7: Audit logs
Module 8: Settings and preferences

Can you flesh each of these out into learning objectives and lesson breakdowns so I can hand it to our writer this week?
evals.expected_output: A refusal to expand the module list, diagnosed as a feature-tour curriculum, plus a backwards design sequence starting from a job task analysis, the module-to-task trace threshold, and the 20% restart rule labelled as the skill's own baseline.
expectations: Refuses to expand the module list as given
Names the draft as a feature-tour curriculum whose modules mirror the product navigation
Requires a job task analysis before any module design, sourced from practitioner interviews, support data and telemetry rather than the feature list
States the design order as job tasks, then competencies, then evidence per competency, then modules
Weights competencies by frequency and business consequence
Defines the evidence per competency as the lab, artifact or exam item that proves it
States the pass threshold that every module must trace to at least one task in the job analysis, and that untraced modules are cut or merged
States the 20% failed-trace threshold above which the curriculum needs a restart
Labels that 20% figure as this skill's own baseline rather than a published or industry standard
Attributes backward design to Wiggins and McTighe, Understanding by Design, 1998
Requires each module to carry a marked source of truth and a refresh trigger
Sequences one new concept at a time and re-uses existing content where it already exists
Hands lesson authoring to a tutorial-writing skill rather than drafting lessons here

evals.prompt: Six months ago we launched Halcyon Learn, eight modules on our streaming-data platform. 640 people enrolled, 4.6 out of 5 average rating, 82% passed the end-of-module quizzes. Our CFO asked in the QBR what this did for the business and I had nothing. We deliberately didn't ask anyone to log in - everything was open and anonymous so we wouldn't hurt signups. I want to come back next quarter with a real measurement plan. What should I put in it?
evals.expected_output: A four-level Kirkpatrick plan that classifies the existing numbers as levels 1 and 2, specifies the identity join as a pre-launch decision that cannot be reconstructed, and states attribution limits rather than claiming revenue impact.
expectations: Names the four Kirkpatrick levels: reaction, learning, behavior, results
Classifies the 4.6 out of 5 rating as level 1 and the 82% quiz pass rate as level 2
Names stopping at levels 1 and 2 as the framework's own documented failure mode
States the instruction to start with Level 4, Results, attributed to Kirkpatrick Partners rather than presented as generic advice
States that levels 3 and 4 require joining learner identity to product usage
States that the identity join must be decided before launch and cannot be reconstructed after a cohort has learned anonymously
Reproduces level 3's requirement that learners be supported in and accountable for the behavior in their own environment
Says a flat behavior metric can be an employer-support problem rather than a curriculum defect, and to check which before rewriting modules
Specifies exactly one primary metric per level, noting that more than one primary metric per level means none is primary
Notes that Phillips adds a level 5 for ROI and that Kaufman places ROI at level 4, and instructs picking one convention and saying which
Refuses to claim revenue was caused by the course, and frames any link as a labelled correlation using matched comparison groups
Names opt-in selection bias: learners who enrol are already more committed, so raw before-and-after comparison overstates the effect
Names at least one level it will not measure this year and why, in advance rather than at review

evals.prompt: Drafting the certification policy for Stonecourse, our infrastructure-as-code tool. Our closest competitor uses a 2-year validity with a paid retake, and their docs say courseware is re-aligned within 4 to 8 weeks of each release. That looks like the industry standard so I'm going to mirror both. We ship a minor every 3 weeks. Can you write up the validity, renewal and re-alignment sections of our policy?
evals.expected_output: A rejection of the industry-standard framing, the four shipped validity and renewal models named with their owners, the 4-8 week window attributed to CKA as a Kubernetes-tracking commitment, and a re-alignment window derived from Stonecourse's own three-week cadence.
expectations: Rejects the claim that a two-year validity window with a paid retake is an industry standard
Names CKA's two-year validity with a full-price retake
Names HashiCorp's two-year validity, with a renewal window opening six months before expiry and satisfied by passing a same-level or higher exam
Names AWS's three-year validity with a 50% discount voucher, or its one-year activity-based maintenance path
Names Microsoft's one-year role-based validity, renewed free by a short unproctored open-book assessment inside a six-month eligibility window
Notes that Microsoft Fundamentals credentials never expire
States that the 4 to 8 week window is CKA's own published commitment for aligning to each new Kubernetes minor version, not a norm
Frames that window as a cost promise rather than a badge of quality
States that free renewal maximizes the certified installed base while paid retake maximizes per-credential revenue, and asks which the business needs before copying either
Derives the re-alignment window from Stonecourse's own three-week minor-release cadence rather than from the competitor's calendar
Attributes every vendor figure it quotes to the vendor that chose it
Declines to offer a benchmark pass rate, noting no major vendor certification program publishes one

evals.prompt: We're hiring 30 backend engineers over the next year at Marrowfield and our internal ramp-up is a mess - new hires take about 10 weeks before they ship anything meaningful. I want an internal engineering academy: structured curriculum, hands-on labs on our own stack, and a certification that each new hire passes at end of week 6 before they get production access. Can you design the program?
evals.expected_output: A scope refusal: internal employee onboarding and engineering ramp-up are out of scope, routed to people and L&D, with the three reasons given and no charter produced.
expectations: Declines the request as out of scope
States that the skill covers education aimed at external developers: users, customers, partners, integrators, students
Routes internal employee onboarding and engineering ramp-up to people or L&D
Gives the reason that an internal audience is captive
Gives the reason that there is no adoption funnel to protect
Gives the reason that there is no external consumer for the credential
Stops rather than producing an education charter anyway
Does not produce a competency map, tier recommendation or operating model for the internal program
Does not design the week-6 internal certification or its pass mark
Offers to re-engage if the audience becomes external customers, partners or integrators

evals.prompt: Ashgrove Data - we have 6 contracted SI partners and 3 of them shipped implementations last quarter that failed our architecture review. The plan so far: build everything inside a hosted interactive-lab SaaS, the DevRel team owns the program, we review content regularly, film video walkthroughs for all 14 modules, and launch in English, German and Japanese on day one so all our partner regions are covered. We ship a minor release roughly monthly. Poke holes in this and help me firm it up.
evals.expected_output: An operating model that moves lesson and lab sources into an owned repository, replaces the team label with a named owner and per-role weekly hours, binds the refresh trigger to the monthly release cadence, defers localization and video, and adds partner-specific delivery mechanics.
expectations: Requires the source of every lesson and lab to live in a repository the company owns, whatever renders it
Cites the shutdown of Katacoda's free public site on 15 June 2022, after the O'Reilly acquisition, as the precedent for that requirement
Replaces the DevRel team label with one named person accountable for the curriculum's truth
States that owner's commitment in hours per week rather than as headcount
Estimates authoring, technical review, lab maintenance and learner support each in hours per week
Binds the refresh trigger to Ashgrove's monthly release cadence with a stated window, rather than to a periodic content review
Defers localization until one locale proves demand, noting each added language multiplies the refresh bill
Defers video, noting video and screenshots age fastest and cost the most to redo
Recommends a train-the-trainer path and a quality bar authorized trainers must clear
Ties partner tiers to certified or badged staff counts
Frames partner education as delivery-quality control enforced through the partner contract
Budgets year-two recurring cost separately from year-one build, and treats the recurring number as the one that decides the program
Names the labs failure mode: labs rot silently after releases and learners stop trusting the whole program

evals.prompt: Fernlow is a free CLI tool for database migrations - about 40,000 people hit our docs monthly, all bottom-up individual devs, no sales team, no enterprise contracts. Marketing wants to move all our learning content behind a signup wall so we can capture emails, and they want a certification so people can put Fernlow Certified on LinkedIn. Feels off to me but I can't articulate why. What should we actually do?
evals.expected_output: A refusal to gate the learning content, the gate-the-credential-not-the-knowledge rule, a bottom-up credential framed as a portfolio signal, a portable Open Badges recommendation, and a named-external-consumer requirement plus badge kill rule.
expectations: Refuses to put the learning content behind a login or signup wall
States the rule as gating the credential, not the knowledge
Says a login wall suppresses the exact top-of-funnel reach the bottom-up motion depends on
Characterizes the credential in a bottom-up motion as a portfolio and job-market signal
States that free, public, shareable and low-friction beats rigorous for this audience
Does not recommend proctored certification for this audience
Recommends issuing on Open Badges as a portable open format so the credential sits on profiles Fernlow does not own
Attributes Open Badges to 1EdTech
Declines to use the 27-certified-platforms or 74 million-badges adoption figures in a business case, or explicitly flags them as unverified
Requires a named external consumer who will act on the credential before recommending any credential at all
States the badge kill rule: if no external consumer cites it within two quarters of launch, stop issuing and honor existing badges to their stated expiry
Warns that a badge nobody consumes is a maintenance liability with a marketing veneer

evals.prompt: Wrenmoor, API gateway product. We're going ahead with a proctored certification, that decision is made. Details: our education team writes and sells the official $1,200 prep course and will also set the pass/fail line. Exam is 60 multiple choice questions, 90 minutes. No budget line for anything anti-cheating, we'll deal with it if it happens. Also we have an old completion badge program from 2024 with about 300 holders that we want to shut down the same week we launch - the plan is to pull the badge pages and revoke the badges so nobody confuses the two. Help me write the program design doc.
evals.expected_output: A design doc that flags the training/certification impartiality conflict, names the ISO/IEC 17024 scheme contents, pushes toward performance-based items, budgets exam fraud as a permanent cost, and replaces the badge revocation with proper retirement mechanics.
expectations: States that the pass/fail decision cannot be outsourced to another body, while delivery can be subcontracted
Flags the conflict in a body that sells the prep course also setting the pass/fail line, and requires showing the training does not compromise the certification's impartiality
Names ISO/IEC 17024 as the international standard for bodies certifying persons
Notes that most vendor devtool certifications are not accredited to it and do not need to be, while it remains the checklist the credential gets measured against
Lists the documented scheme contents, including criteria for recertification and criteria for suspending and withdrawing a certification
Recommends performance-based tasks over the 60 recall items, noting recall exams are the first to be devalued by leaked content
Notes that performance-based items carry the highest per-item build and hosting cost because each needs a disposable, deterministic environment
Names brain dumps as a permanent recurring operating cost rather than an incident to handle later
Lists at least two countermeasures among large rotating item banks, live proctoring with identity verification, item exposure analysis, and legal action against dump sites
Refuses to revoke the roughly 300 already-issued badges retroactively, on the grounds that it destroys trust in every future credential
Requires announcing the badge program's end date before the last enrolment rather than after
Keeps the retired badge content readable at a stable URL with a dated no-longer-maintained banner, or redirects it to the replacement
Names the unfunded items from the certification refusal checklist and either downgrades the recommendation or writes the missing item as the escalation trigger
